title: Paranoia and Conspiracy Theories in Hollywood

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Part 05: From 1970 to 1989. Chapter 6: Paranoia and Conspiracy Theories in Hollywood.
segments.text: Part zero five: From nineteen seventy to nineteen eighty-nine. Chapter six: Paranoia and Conspiracy Theories in Hollywood.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 1970s were troubled, paranoid years, and Hollywood couldn't help but mirror that on screen.
segments.text: The nineteen seventies were troubled, paranoid years, and Hollywood couldn't help but mirror that on screen.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The production of political and psychological thrillers in 1970s Hollywood is generally interpreted as a paranoid reaction to the Watergate scandal and a residue of the witch hunt against communists in the 1950s. Other contributing factors include the specter of the Vietnam War and the feeling among liberals that, although everyone hated the war, it went on because of the government's stubbornness.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: There was a growing sense that Hollywood did not understand its audience. All of this combined left the film world insecure and the nation introspective. The prototype of Hollywood conspiracy films is The Manchurian Candidate (1962), directed by John Frankenheimer (1920-2002). While seemingly about a communist plot against the American government, the film reveals that the conspiracy is the work of homegrown politicians and military leaders. During the 1960s and 1970s, films portraying the authorities as ambiguous and corrupt became common.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: However, Hollywood's paranoia peaked with the Watergate scandal in 1972. A definite sense of unease became visible in many Hollywood genres: in Westerns such as Pat Garrett & Billy the Kid (1973), political dramas such as The Candidate (1972), gangster films such as The Godfather Part II (1974), and science fiction works such as Soylent Green (1973). In each of them, the forces of American power and politics are portrayed as untrustworthy, exploiting ordinary people for personal or corporate gain.

Pakula (1928-1998) in which the hippie reporter played by Warren Beatty (b. 1937) investigates the Kennedy-style assassination of a committed American senator and stumbles upon a plot that reaches the highest echelons of business and government.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The film set the stylistic template for the conspiracy film: labyrinthine narrative, booming sound effects, overlapping dialogue, brutal steel-and-glass architecture, and sparing use of music on the soundtrack. The Conversation (1974), directed by Francis Ford Coppola (b. 1939), and Night Moves (1975), by Arthur Penn (1922-2010), adopt an equally cold, modernist style but tell more intimate stories. Both films star Gene Hackman as a private investigator who confronts forces far beyond his control and loses his identity in the process.

segments.original: In these films, the doomed hero, though intelligent and committed, becomes a victim not only of powerful outside influences but also of his own emotional weakness, his instability, and his obsessive nature.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The only film to deal directly with the Watergate scandal was All the President's Men (1976). Despite its narrative complexity and fact-packed screenplay, the film was a hit with an audience desperate to leave the Nixon era behind. After it, with Nixon defeated and the Vietnam War over, paranoia began to give way to the optimism of films such as Star Wars (1977). Traces remained in works such as Marathon Man (1976), directed by John Schlesinger (1926-2003), although the corrupting force in that film belongs not to a rotten government organization but to an individual, in the form of a Nazi war criminal.
